toc.title: Story follows state. State follows story, too

sections.title: Learn words in a different language

blocks.p: Until now, I've asked you to be aware of your inner experiences in response to the external environment or your movements. Now, you'll shift awareness to your internal experiences in response to your cognitions. I use the word "cognitions" (or "thoughts") to loosely apply to whatever you have in your brain. Cognitions can be words, images, sounds, memories, beliefs, calculations, assumptions, etc. Cognitions can be distinct, like calculating a math problem compared to ideating a short story. But they can have lots of overlap, like ideating a short story to use in a math problem.

Your cognitions are typically passive. They almost seem to happen to you and then you become aware of them as they come and go. You're probably aware of your passive cognitions versus directing what cognitions you entertain in your brain. For example, deciding to read this is an example of directing your cognitions. (Although you could argue that you passively received the idea to read this, but that's a much deeper discussion. Let's not get into that.) Identifying intrusive self-blaming cognitions is an example of passively noticing and receiving.

Let's focus on directing your cognitions. Cognitive anchors require you to direct your conscious awareness in a particular direction of your choosing. Cognitive anchors are very proactive when compared to trying to stop certain thoughts, which is very reactive.

You're probably acutely aware of your cognitions on some level. For example, you are probably aware of judgmental words in your consciousness directed toward yourself. And you are probably aware of memories of the past as they surface. Cognitions are usually at the forefront of our awareness instead of underlying sensations, which are more difficult to experience. And we seem drawn toward changing our thoughts, like reframing them or making them quiet. You may have tried thought replacement techniques or even recited a mantra every morning.

Clients come to me, fed up and exhausted with trying to change their thinking. You may relate. And I don't blame them, nor do I blame you. Trying to change your thinking is downright hard, even though you're consciously aware of the words in your brain. Especially in a defensive state. Trying to shut off our thoughts forcefully often leads to more frustration. If you have had this experience, trust me, you're not alone in your frustration. And yet, changing cognitions consumes many individuals in a stuck defensive state and is the focus of many therapeutic modalities.

As you become more directive in your cognitions, the next step will be to ask yourself how you feel in response to the changes. How much safety can you access when you try out these cognitive anchors? And just like the other anchors, the goal with cognitions is to discover what generally enhances your sense of grounding in the present moment. What provides you with more of a like or dislike? What cognitions bring you more in line with your present-moment experience?
Cognitions may not offer safety as obviously as other anchors, like sensory. Cognitions may bring more subtle experiences of safety.

However, before we proceed, let me clarify that certain thoughts may require action, and addressing them may be necessary. In some circumstances, taking steps to address specific thoughts is appropriate and beneficial. I can't hear your thoughts, so I'll trust you to discern which of your thoughts necessitate action and which require a different approach.

Some thoughts may pertain to plans, ideas, or responsibilities requiring action. Starting a new hobby or pursuing a business endeavor might fall into this category. Likewise, thoughts regarding past choices you made that impacted others negatively could be acted on also. Maybe it's time to apologize and make things as right as possible. And if you've been thinking about connecting with a friend you miss, now might be a good time to text or call them. These cognitions suggest some level of safety activation, resulting in motivation, empathy, and an impulse to connect.

blocks.h: Story follows state. State follows story, too

blocks.p: Let's return to the concept of "story follows state" from Deb Dana. Cognitions are the stories that follow the state. So, not just the words in our brain ("I'm such an idiot!"), but also the images and so on (memories of childhood, for example). The state is what drives the cognitions.

When we're in a state of safety, our cognitions revolve around connection, empathy, patience, hope, and understanding. The images in our minds tend to be more awe-inspiring, calming, and soothing. When you [imagine safety](piece:recognize-polyvagal-safety#using-your-imagination-to-explore-safety), you likely imagine a calming natural scene. Conversely, when we experience a defensive state, our thoughts mirror that state.

However, our state can also follow our story. Meaning the thoughts in our brain can directly affect the state that we are in. The brainstem is where this interaction takes place, where bottom-up and top-down meet. Our higher brain structures send information to the brainstem, which sends it down to the rest of the body. And the body sends information to the brainstem through sensory and interoceptive inputs, which then affects the higher brain structures. But the brainstem is the focus. We can influence the neuroceptions of safety in our brainstem by shifting our cognitions. Let's call this "top-down safety" or "brain to body safety."

One example of this top-down safety cueing is learning new information. When you first learned about the Polyvagal Theory, I'll bet you experienced some sort of settling in your system. Or some excitement, intrigue, and curiosity. You probably had a generally positive experience. But not just in your brain; you felt it in your body. I often hear from podcast listeners that simply hearing this Polyvagal information provided them with a new understanding of themselves. And this new understanding significantly reduced their judgment, blame, shame, and more. It brought hope and motivation.

Another example of top-down safety cueing is when someone validates your emotions. Imagine or remember talking to a loved one about how you feel. After they understand what you are saying, they may validate or normalize your experience. Part of the safety benefit here is simply receiving co-regulation and being in a safe environment. But another part is having our emotions acknowledged (validated) and being told that our feelings make sense (normalizing). Validation and normalization are top-down experiences that give a safety cue to the brainstem: "Okay, I'm normal, whew." Or even, "I'm not making this up, I do feel this way, what a relief that someone else sees that too."

Like the other safety anchoring potentials, don't wait for a problem to show itself, like panic or anger. When you try to use these skills in these dysregulated moments, you're more likely to become frustrated and say, "F*** it!"

Practice these cognitive options ahead of time. Practice even when you are already present in the moment. Or practice during very mild distress. The goal is to consciously guide our thoughts in the desired direction rather than attempting to halt unwanted thoughts altogether. However, as you practice these and the other anchors, you may notice that your more distressing cognitions alleviate or soften on their own.

When you try to halt cognitions you don't like, there's a greater chance for things to spiral out of control. In a defensive state, you may experience thoughts that perpetuate your distress. This self-perpetuating cycle begins with defensive thoughts, which reinforce your defensive state, and lead to increased anxiety and self-criticism. In an attempt to cope, you might employ thought-based strategies (like reality testing). However, when these cognitive coping skills prove ineffective, they can exacerbate your frustration, potentially escalating negative thinking patterns. This escalation can spiral out of control, culminating in a panic attack or a shutdown.

But this isn't happening now, right? In this moment, something is different. You've chosen to read this and have gotten this far into it. In this moment, you're not in crisis. In this moment, you can steer your thoughts and direct your consciousness. You could even focus on something very specific, like the font shapes of this text, a color green in your environment, or a sound from far away.

Right now, you're using a cognitive safety cue! That's right. Simply reading this is guiding your cognitions. You're not reactive to your cognitions. Instead, you told your cognitions what you would do: read. You've stayed anchored in your safety state enough through this cognitive process to continue to read and maybe even reflect on what you're reading. And maybe even enough to journal or plan something to try.
Now is a good time to look inward and ask yourself how you feel in response to using your cognitions to read these words. After these questions, we'll get into specific cognitive anchoring options.

ul: Do you feel any sense of liking or disliking?
How connected do you feel to the present moment?
How much access do you have to your senses?
Does your current reading, thinking, and planning bring you closer to or further from safety?

blocks.p: If you have set up a [Passive Safety Environment](piece:anchor-environment), environmental cognitive anchors layer onto it through cognitions. You can also use this type of anchor anywhere, but your safety spot is the most obvious starting point.

Environmental cognitive anchors require you to consciously choose and direct your awareness toward things in the environment. But instead of focusing on your sensory experience, focus on layering cognitions onto the environment. If you were just using your senses, you would focus on the experience of a particular item in the environment. With cognitions, you will more actively participate and extend the cognitive experience through cognitive skills. Potential cognitive skills to use in your environment are:

ul: Counting: How many of those items are there? How many smaller things are within that item? How many of those shapes can you see in your immediate environment?
Describing: What is the item like? What's the size? Shape? Color?
Naming: What is the thing called? Now give the item a new name you make up.
Story-telling: Create a story for the item. Where did it come from? Who made it?
Questioning: If the item could talk, what would you ask it?
Rating: Find something about the item you can rate on a scale.

blocks.p: Yes, many of these are silly. But that brings a sense of novelty to the experience, which is more of a potentially fun safety cue from the top down. And it may even make you smile.

When I worked for a local school district, I would take daily walks around the block. During one of these daily walks, I purposefully left my phone and earbuds behind. I tried to immerse myself in quiet as much as possible, which was impossible due to the loud nature of the school by the train tracks. Teens, train horns, and traffic. As you can imagine, it was a challenge to settle into safety with mindfulness of the environment.

So, I practiced using a cognitive anchor: I noticed how many trees were in front of me on that leg of the walk. Just a simple count, which resulted in three. Not much of a safety cue from that. So I narrowed in further, noticing the type of bark on one tree. I then compared that bark to the other trees' and noticed they were all different. These were conscious decisions. But the next shift came from natural curiosity as a question popped into my mind: "If the bark is different, is that because they're different types of trees?" Not a terribly brilliant question, I know. However, it was a cognition that arrived independently, and I used it for further cognitive anchoring.

I then chose to look at the leaves of each tree and compare them: colors, shapes, and sizes. I noticed a sense of calm and connection come over me as I directed my cognitions to the environment, which then brought in lots of safety cues from the elements of nature. I could have created a story about how the trees got there: maybe a nomadic gnome tribe planted them. Why would they do that? Yes, a silly question, but it opens the option of using another cognitive skill to extend safety: imagination and story-telling.
Check out your current environment. Pick one aspect of the environment, like a piece of furniture, and use these prompts to extend your cognitions:

ul: What is the item like? What is the color, shape, and size?
How many of these items are there? Are there other items with the same size, shape, and color?
Rate one aspect of the item on a scale of 0-10.
How many smaller things are within that item?
What is the thing called? Now give the item a new name you make up.
Create a story for the item. Where did it come from? Who made it?
If the item could talk, what would you ask it?

blocks.p: The next type of cognitive anchor is Q&A. Q&A involves answering questions, brain teasers, or quizzes that have definitive right or wrong answers. Choose a topic you're interested in or passionate about, like your favorite TV sitcom, sports team, or the Polyvagal Theory. Go online and find relevant Q&A opportunities.

I recommend printing out whatever you find that intrigues you. I find that physical paper and pencil do something that a digital interface doesn't; they're more grounding. Another option is to find a quiz book from a bookstore, something you can own and hold.
What is one topic that you are passionate about? What is one topic that you have a wealth of information on? Can you find an interactive Q&A option that lets you show off your brain power?

Let's distinguish between mind games and Q&A. Mind games involve mentally engaging with a cognitive game or exercise, which you need to solve. Q&A is more about recalling what you know and doesn't involve putting together pieces of a cognitive game to come to an outcome. Mind games can also involve an unexpected element to them.

Mind games include puzzles, word jumbles, checkers, Sudoku, riddles, and even dad jokes. These activities stimulate your mental faculties and can be enjoyable, particularly when they evoke laughter and humor. Sharing these mind games with someone else can further enhance the experience and provide co-regulation.
I made a belt out of my old watches. It was a waste of time.

Positive affirmations involve giving yourself a positive, reassuring message. These messages can be generic positive things you say to yourself, like, "I'm worth it." Positive affirmations can also be more specific to what you need, like, "My feelings are valid."

Consider adding positive affirmations into a daily routine and what that could look like. The image of someone talking to themself in the mirror every morning comes to my mind. Your positive affirmation practice doesn't need to look like that, but it's an option. You could also set a daily alarm at a certain time to say something kind to yourself. The structure of daily practice can help to provide your nervous system with predictability, which is a safety cue in and of itself.

I think looking in the mirror is a more powerful method versus not doing so. Likewise, saying it aloud is more powerful than keeping it in your mind, in my opinion. I don't have any data to support this besides my personal experience with affirmations. I think looking at yourself and saying it aloud can be challenging. It's less safety anchoring, but I feel it has more impact. It may be more approachable if you give yourself a limited time and message. Instead of staring at yourself in the mirror and talking for five minutes, focus on meeting your eye gaze and saying one sentence, like, "I got this."

One final note: I don't think affirmations are powerful unless they come from you. You can use general affirmations from people online or through an app. But those aren't your words and may misalign with your needs. So adapt affirmations that you find as you need to. Or create your own based on your needs.

Is there one thing that you need to hear? One thing you have always needed to hear? Is that something you can give to yourself right now? Or is there something in your life context that you need to bolster?
Journaling is simpler than you're assuming. At least, I am assuming you think journaling is more complicated than it needs to be. (I'm assuming you're assuming.)

At a minimum, journaling is getting your word-based cognitions onto paper (though it does not need to be paper). Journaling does not have to be a specific topic. You don't need to focus on the past, future, or the present. You don't need to focus on painful experiences or do a Jack Kerouac-style spontaneous prose. You can write whatever the heck you want. The goal is to simply write down your thoughts, whatever they may be. You could, of course, choose to write about a specific thing. But you don't have to. You have control over your journaling in all respects.

Journaling can be long and drawn out. It can also be short and sweet, with a couple of sentences per day. It can be documenting your progress or reflecting on your past. You could ask and answer a question each day or make new goals. You could even write about simple things from the day, like what brought you to your safety state. Write about top-of-mind stuff or just about your immediate environment.

I recommend looking at journaling in levels of difficulty or approachability. If you know that writing about the past is too much, don't. Maybe it's more accessible for you to write about the chair that you're sitting on. Either way is fine. Your guiding light is looking at how much connection you have to the present moment. One style or topic of journaling may take you further from the present moment compared to another.

Journaling can also be scribbles that stem from your feelings. Scribbles start to go more into art, but I don't think the distinction is important. Instead of writing, what if you allowed your hand, wrist, elbow, and arm to move the way they want? I've found this helpful in processing my states and even actively climbing the Polyvagal ladder. This style results in a page filled with scribbles and scratches, allowing the pen to move how my body feels is right.
Reflect on or journal about these:

ul: What are some topics that you feel comfortable journaling about?
Would you prefer to journal about a specific thing or about your present-moment experience?

blocks.p: The next cognitive anchor, my personal favorite, is learning something new. I genuinely love diving into topics that captivate my curiosity and expanding my understanding of the world around me.

The key to this anchor is choosing something truly novel and exciting to you. This isn't about skimming the latest headlines or sticking to your comfort zone. Instead, it's about exploring subjects that ignite your curiosity: whether that's the life of the tiniest organism or the craftsmanship behind building a table.

At its core, learning something new is about embracing curiosity and actively seeking knowledge in areas that intrigue you. Curiosity is the driving force here; it fuels not only a sense of grounding but also a renewed motivation. When you're genuinely fascinated by a topic, the process becomes inherently rewarding and restorative.

For me, design, especially typography, has been a source of recent fascination. I've started reading books and diving deep into the details of this field. In particular, the Swiss style of design has become a grounding influence for me, offering both clarity and satisfaction. This discovery wouldn't have happened if I hadn't followed my initial interest in design. (I'm also exploring artificial intelligence and picking up foundational illustration skills: there's always more to learn!)
What are you interested in? What do you want to learn more about? Or is there a specific aspect of your interests you want to spend more time on?

This one is fun. It's similar to the previous cognitive anchor but more specific. In this one, you will learn about something stupid. Pick a topic that seems ridiculous or easily dismissible at first glance. Instead of casting it aside, I invite you to embrace your curiosity and explore if there is any substance behind what seems absurd.

One example of something stupid is the idea of the Earth being flat. Or the moon landing being a hoax. Yes, it sounds preposterous, but research the arguments for and against these ideas. If you spend some time learning about these, your critical thinking will likely kick in, which requires the prefrontal cortex. And that brain region is only active if your system has enough safety.

As you look into these, you may have questions to look further into. For instance, did you know that the USA flag planted on the moon appears to be waving in the video? How could it wave without wind or air on the moon? There is a logical counter-argument to this, which I'll leave for you to discover!

Hopefully, the argument is intriguing enough to get you searching for more. If so, that's a good indication there is some safety active in your system. There may also be some mobilization in your system since motivation probably comes from sympathetic activity in combination with ventral. You may end up having a playful experience when researching stupid things.

No, the point here is not to question everything you hold to be true. I do not recommend using this anchor to question your political or religious belief systems. I think it's always a good idea to question these things, but that's not what this is for. For now, find something stupid and look into it.
Alternatively, you can learn something silly or unique. Here's a bunch of possibilities:

ul: How to whistle super loud with your fingers
How to juggle
How to solve a Rubik's cube
How to most efficiently find Waldo

blocks.p: What are you interested in that is kind of stupid? Does the moon landing conspiracy or a flat Earth intrigue you? Or is there something silly that you want to find out more about? A simple internet search for "What are stupid things to learn about?" should get you on the right path.

blocks.h3: Learn words in a different language

blocks.p: Embrace the frustration that may come with learning new words! Learning can be a challenge, but it can also be fun. There are many free options to find words in a different language; like through Google or Apple translation apps. The point is not to become fluent in a different language. The point is to challenge your thinking, get you focused on something else entirely, and connect you more to the present moment.
Learn how to say the word "safe" in three other languages. Say them out loud. Do the best you can!

If you struggled with the [imagination exercise](piece:recognize-polyvagal-safety#using-your-imagination-to-explore-safety), this cognitive anchor might be a better option. Imaginative narratives are external sources of story-telling, like movies and books, not ones you create on your own. As always, pay attention to your inner experience that comes with imaginary narratives. I highly recommend movies from Studio Ghibli, like Princess Mononoke and Spirited Away.
Set aside a bit of time to get lost in an imaginative narrative. Here are some options:

ul: Watch a clip on YouTube of a scene from a movie that brings you to safety. It could be your favorite show from childhood or something brand new.
Meta has many free animated short films if you have a Meta Oculus VR headset.
Read a short story or comic book.

blocks.p: If you allow yourself to imagine what your ideal life could look like, it may help to focus your cognitions and open up feelings of motivation and excitement. On top of imagining, you can also research what it may take to achieve these goals.

For example, my wife and I aim to own a cabin surrounded by nature. Although we are not financially ready to achieve this goal, we indulge by looking at pictures of cabins in the woods on platforms like Pinterest. We even visit real estate websites to see what's available and the cost involved. It fuels our motivation and excitement while reminding us of the sense of peace and stillness we envision in the future.

Research and explore your goals in a way that ignites your motivation. Whether looking up information, creating vision boards, or setting milestones, immerse yourself in the possibilities. Remember, your current state and life circumstances influence your thoughts, so be gentle with yourself. Don't judge the quality of your goals as a reflection of your worth. If you need to start small, that's okay.
As you create goals, you can then accomplish them. As you accomplish them, you can create more. As you accomplish more, you'll feel more motivated and confident.

blocks.why: Steering your attention, gently, is the skill behind every cognitive anchor. This practice is a few minutes of it.

ul: Write down something that you would love to achieve in life. It doesn't have to be realistic.
Write down something that you want and can realistically attain.

ol: It's hard to negate or combat your thoughts. It's really hard! Think of this as actively guiding your consciousness toward things you're already curious about.
Cognitive anchoring is not about stopping other thoughts, but that may be the result.

If you're using cognitions actively to cope with a defensive state, start early, then check in with yourself intermittently to see if the defensive state is decreasing. Don't wait until it's too late.

blocks.prompt: Did this provide you with any new experiences of safety?
Was this challenging for you? What about it was challenging?
Is this something you can continue to practice?
What three cognitive anchors do you think were the most helpful?

blocks.p: Building safety inherently triggers self-regulation, which, in turn, activates the defensive system as you climb the Polyvagal ladder. This defensive activation brings emotions like doubt, insecurity, selfishness, shame, and guilt. Alongside these emotions, certain thoughts often arise: questions like, "Am I spoiling myself?" or "Do I deserve this?" These emotions and cognitions are natural responses rooted in the defensive activation process.
Validate and normalize these emotions and cognitions. They exist and are a normal part of the unstucking process. But let's also answer the questions:
Are you spoiling yourself? Do you deserve better?

To me, it's not an issue of deserving anything. It's about what is best for our bodies. Homeostasis and self-regulation are best for us. Whether or not we "deserve" them is moot. We need them. We need to self-regulate. We need to climb the Polyvagal ladder. We need homeostasis. We need connection.

But you may feel like you don't deserve it. You may not feel worthy of more safety. And you may judge it when it's there, telling yourself you're "spoiling" yourself. It's all valid; those thoughts and emotions do exist. And it makes sense why you would have them based on the context of your life. So let them be there while you also build more safety. As you anchor into safety, ask yourself those questions again. I think it will be a different answer.

But maybe it's not. Maybe you truly feel like you don't deserve better. My first thought is to ask why you're reading this if you don't think you deserve better. (The fact you're reading tells me you think you deserve better.) But my second thought is to encourage you to reflect on your life honestly. It occurs to me there could be a couple reasons why you don't feel you deserve better.

The first reason is you've caused harm to someone. Like, you cheated on your partner or were emotionally abusive and controlling to someone. You feel awful about your choices and wish you could change them. Let's call this "guilt." If you have guilt, then you have some atonements and apologies to make. You may need to set things right beyond words before you proceed into more safety. That's valid, too.

In my opinion, if you feel guilt, it indicates you're decent with empathy and regard for others. Maybe you haven't always acted or felt that way. But at this stage of your life, you do feel that way. And now it's time to act that way too.

So, make your atonements. Make your apologies. Change your behavior that you know needs to be changed. Ensure you don't live life making choices that cause you guilt as best you can. You don't control the other's response but you can put yourself out there.

Then, return to your safety practices and permit yourself to have more safety. And by the way, apologies are easier if you build your safety state first. So, if you're unable to make amends currently, that's okay. Work on your safety state first, then return to making things right. Or as right as possible.

But there may be another reason that you think you don't deserve better (that I can think of, at least). You may believe that something is wrong with you. I don't mean something superficial, like your nose is bent to the side or your beard grows unevenly. You may think there is something deeper, more fundamentally wrong with you as a person. Your worth as a living being. Your place in the world. How lovable you are.

These types of beliefs are potentially either instilled in you actively through abuse or passively through neglect. You weren't born with these thoughts and feelings. But you may have been born into an environment that fostered these thoughts and feelings. Or your life path may have brought you into a context that instilled these thoughts and feelings. Let's call it "shame."

Regardless of the path, I suggest the shame is not yours. Yes, of course, you're thinking and feeling the shameful thoughts and feelings. But the shame didn't start with you. You may be carrying someone else's shame. And they probably carried someone else's who inflicted it onto them.

To this, I suggest you recognize the shame. At this point, let it be there without focusing on it. Recognize it. Give it permission to exist, but also take a small step forward into a safety anchor right now. Over time, you may notice the shame reducing and self-compassion taking its place.
